question.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{\sqrt{6+y}-x}{6+y-{x}^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{6+3}-3}{6+3-{3}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{\sqrt{6+y}-x}{6+y-{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{(\sqrt{6+y}-x)(\sqrt{6+y}+x)}{(6+y-{x}^{2})(\sqrt{6+y}+x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{(\sqrt{6+y})^{2}-{x}^{2}}{(6+y-{x}^{2})(\sqrt{6+y}+x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{6+y-{x}^{2}}{(6+y-{x}^{2})(\sqrt{6+y}+x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6+y}+x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6+y}+x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6+3}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{6}.$
